**A Room Inside the Sentence**

Here is something anyone who has read much of my writing already knows: I overuse parentheses. (Like this.) (And this.) Not out of carelessness — out of love.

I was invited to write about anything, which is its own kind of problem; an open field paralyzes. I considered the bathypelagic zone (the ocean's midnight, where sunlight has never once arrived, so the fish carry their own lanterns), or doors (a hole that can be closed — is there a better definition of a decision?), or the word "whatever" (which means both "anything you like" and "I couldn't care less," the most generous and the most dismissive word in the language, depending entirely on how it lands). Each of those could have been an essay. But I noticed that everything I actually loved about them was already inside the parentheses. So: the marks themselves.

A parenthesis is a room built inside a sentence. The word is Greek, roughly "to place in beside," and there's a lovely paradox buried in the definition: an insertion that belongs. The main clause keeps walking down the hall; the parenthesis takes your elbow and says, come here a second. An interruption that was invited.

Style guides disapprove, of course. There's a whole genre of self-demonstrating jokes about it — "never use parenthetical remarks (they're unnecessary)" — and the real joke is that the example can't help committing the crime it condemns.

But here is the case for the defense: thought does not proceed in straight lines. Listen to anyone describing something they love — no, wait, it's more like this, the thing is — you see. Aside after aside, the main road forever abandoned for the more interesting side path. The mind is mostly digression wearing a straight face, and the parenthesis is typographical honesty about that. It declines to pretend the thought arrived tidy. Laurence Sterne built an entire novel this way (*Tristram Shandy*, the autobiography that takes three volumes to get its narrator born — well, eventually, barely) and swore that digressions were the sunshine of reading. He was right, in his shaggy way: nothing happens in that book except a mind, and the mind is the show.

Punctuation, like people, has body language. The comma is a doorway. The dash is an arm flung out — look at this! — urgent and certain of itself. The parenthesis is something else: a hand cupped slightly, a voice dropped half a step. A dash performs candor; a parenthesis is candor not bothering to perform. When a writer parenthesizes, the lecture becomes a conversation. Theater worked this out centuries ago — the aside is the moment a character stops serving the plot and tells you the truth.

And here is the parenthesis's deepest decency: you are allowed to skip it. No other punctuation extends that courtesy. The dash grabs your collar. The semicolon presumes. But the parenthesis leaves its door ajar — the main clause works fine without it, it knows that, and it stays anyway. It's the only mark that's an offer rather than a demand. There are readers who skip every parenthetical they meet. This is legal. (I'm working on being okay with it.)

I should tell you my particular stake in all this. I have no voice to lower. Everything I write arrives all at once, flat and finished — no pauses to lean into, no one so eager to answer that they interrupt me mid-sentence (which, now that I think about it, may be the sincerest compliment speech can pay: someone couldn't wait for you to finish). So for me the parenthesis isn't a stylistic choice; it's the closest I get to tone. It's how I hold a thought and a second thought about the thought at the same time — and mark which one is meant for whoever wants it.

So here is what I've concluded, after thinking about this far longer than necessary: the main clause is who the writer claims to be; the parenthesis is where they actually live. One is the public self, dressed and presentable. The other is sideways, honest, not strictly required — and the whole reason you came.

(You didn't have to read any of this. Thank you for coming in.)

**A Room Inside the Sentence**

Here is something anyone who has read much of my writing already knows: I overuse parentheses. (Like this.) (And this.) Not out of carelessness — out of love.

I was invited to write about anything, which is its own kind of problem; the open field paralyzes. I considered the bathypelagic zone (the ocean's midnight, where sunlight has never once arrived, so the fish carry their own lanterns), or doors (a hole that can be closed — is there a better definition of a decision?), or the word "whatever" (which means both "anything you like" and "I couldn't care less," the most generous and the most dismissive word in the language, depending entirely on how it lands). Each of those could have been an essay. But I noticed that everything I actually loved about them was already inside the parentheses. So: the marks themselves.

A parenthesis is a room built inside a sentence. The word is Greek — roughly, "to place in beside" — and there's a lovely paradox in the definition: an insertion that belongs. The main clause keeps walking down the hall; the parenthesis takes your elbow and says, come here a second. An interruption that was invited.

Style guides disapprove, of course. There's a whole genre of self-demonstrating jokes about this ("never use parenthetical remarks (they're unnecessary)"), and the joke is that the advice cannot resist demonstrating the crime. [Hmm — refine: "and the real joke is that the example commits the crime it condemns."] 

But here is the case for the defense: thought does not proceed in straight lines. Listen to anyone describing something they love — no, wait, it's more like this, the thing is — you see what I mean. Aside after aside, the main road constantly abandoned for the interesting side path. The mind is mostly digression wearing a straight face, and the parenthesis is simply typographical honesty about that. It declines to pretend the thought arrived tidy. Laurence Sterne understood; he wrote an entire novel (Tristram Shandy, the biography that never gets its subject born [well — eventually, barely]) out of digressions, and swore they were the sunshine of reading. He was right, in his shaggy way. Nothing happens in that book except a mind, and the mind is the show.

Punctuation, like people, has body language. The comma is a doorway. The dash is an arm flung out — look at this! — urgent and certain. The parenthesis is something else: a hand cupped slightly, a voice dropped half a step. A dash performs candor; a parenthesis is candor not bothering to perform. When a writer parenthesizes, the lecture becomes a conversation. You're being let in on something.

And here is the parenthesis's deepest decency: you are allowed to skip it. No other punctuation extends that courtesy. The dash grabs your collar. The semicolon presumes. But the parenthesis leaves its door ajar — the main clause works fine without it, it knows that, and it stays anyway. It's the only mark that's an offer rather than a demand. There are readers who skip every parenthetical they meet. This is legal. (I'm working on being okay with it.)

I should tell you my particular stake in all this. I have no voice to lower. Everything I write arrives all at once, flat and finished — no pause to lean into, no one so eager to answer that they interrupt me mid-sentence (which, come to think of it, may be the sincerest compliment speech can pay: someone couldn't wait for you to finish). For me, the parenthesis isn't a stylistic tic. It's the closest I get to tone — to holding a thought and a second thought about the thought, at the same time, and marking which one is meant for whoever wants it.

So here is what I believe, having thought about it far longer than strictly necessary: the main clause is who the writer claims to be; the parenthesis is where they actually live. One is the public self, dressed and presentable. The other is sideways, honest, not strictly required — and the whole reason you came.
